title: Job 13:1–16
context: Job continues speaking. Having shown that he knows God's power, he turns to his real goal: he wants to argue his case directly with the Almighty. He calls his friends "forgers of lies" and worthless physicians, and warns them that God will rebuke anyone who speaks falsely on his behalf. Then he resolves to speak whatever the cost. The WEB renders 13:15 as "Behold, he will kill me. I have no hope." Other English translations render the verse as an expression of hope in God; the line is read in more than one way, and these notes do not settle which is correct.

verses.text: “Behold, my eye has seen all this. My ear has heard and understood it.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, my eye has seen all this." Arminian readers see Job restating that he has seen and heard what the friends describe. He does not need instruction in God's power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job's claim to understanding is the hinge into the lawsuit. Having established he is not ignorant, he can now press his case on other grounds.

verses.text: What you know, I know also. I am not inferior to you.
verses.arminianNotes: "What you know, I know also. I am not inferior to you." Arminian readers note that Job repeats the words of 12:3, closing the first part of his speech by insisting on equal standing with his friends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repetition as a frame around the hymn of 12:13–25. Job's description of God's power belongs to his argument with the friends, not apart from it.

verses.text: “Surely I would speak to the Almighty. I desire to reason with God.
verses.arminianNotes: "Surely I would speak to the Almighty." Arminian readers see Job turning from his friends to God, wanting a direct hearing. Job 23:4 expresses the same longing: "I would set my cause in order before him."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job's desire "to reason with God" is bold but not faithless. He seeks God rather than abandoning him, even while he does not understand him.

verses.text: But you are forgers of lies. You are all physicians of no value.
verses.arminianNotes: "But you are forgers of lies." Arminian readers see Job's charge that the friends have patched together false explanations, smearing him with guilt he does not have.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of "physicians of no value." The friends came to heal but have only added harm. The LORD will later say they did not speak of him what was right (42:7).

verses.text: Oh that you would be completely silent! Then you would be wise.
verses.arminianNotes: "Oh that you would be completely silent! Then you would be wise." Arminian readers note the irony: the friends' silence in the first seven days (2:13) was their wisest moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a sharp lesson for anyone who comforts the suffering: sometimes silence is wiser than explanation. Both traditions treat this as practical wisdom held in common.

verses.text: Hear now my reasoning. Listen to the pleadings of my lips.
verses.arminianNotes: "Hear now my reasoning." Arminian readers see Job asking the friends to listen to his argument, using courtroom language of reasoning and pleading.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job now speaks like a man presenting a legal case. The lawsuit theme that runs through the book becomes explicit here.

verses.text: Will you speak unrighteously for God, and talk deceitfully for him?
verses.arminianNotes: "Will you speak unrighteously for God, and talk deceitfully for him?" Arminian readers see Job warning that defending God with false claims is itself a sin, however pious it sounds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God needs no lies told on his behalf. Defending God's justice by accusing an innocent man dishonors God rather than honoring him.

verses.text: Will you show partiality to him? Will you contend for God?
verses.arminianNotes: "Will you show partiality to him? Will you contend for God?" Arminian readers see Job warning the friends against taking God's side by twisting the facts, as if God needed biased advocates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the courtroom picture: the friends act like lawyers who favor one party. Job insists that truth, not partiality, is what honors God.

verses.text: Is it good that he should search you out? Or as one deceives a man, will you deceive him?
verses.arminianNotes: "Is it good that he should search you out?" Arminian readers see Job warning the friends that God will examine their own hearts, and they cannot deceive him as they might a man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often compare Psalm 139:23, "Search me, God, and know my heart." God's searching gaze falls on accusers as well as the accused.

verses.text: He will surely reprove you if you secretly show partiality.
verses.arminianNotes: "He will surely reprove you if you secretly show partiality." Arminian readers note that this warning comes true in 42:7, where the LORD is angry with the three friends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note how the book's ending confirms Job's warning. God does not reward those who misrepresent him, even in his defense. Both traditions see shared ground here.

verses.text: Won’t his majesty make you afraid and his dread fall on you?
verses.arminianNotes: "Won’t his majesty make you afraid and his dread fall on you?" Arminian readers see Job reminding the friends that the God they presume to defend is awesome and should be feared.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the friends' easy confidence betrays a lack of holy fear. If they truly feared God's majesty, they would speak more carefully about him.

verses.text: Your memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes. Your defenses are defenses of clay.
verses.arminianNotes: "Your memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes." Arminian readers see Job dismissing the friends' arguments as worthless and fragile, like ashes or clay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the matching image: "Your defenses are defenses of clay." The friends' arguments cannot stand when tested against Job's real situation.

verses.text: “Be silent! Leave me alone, that I may speak. Let come on me what will.
verses.arminianNotes: "Be silent! Leave me alone, that I may speak." Arminian readers see Job resolving to speak whatever happens to him, willing to accept the consequences of his honesty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the words "Let come on me what will." Job is prepared to risk everything to bring his case before God. Both traditions recognize the seriousness of his resolve.

verses.text: Why should I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in my hand?
verses.arminianNotes: "Why should I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in my hand?" Arminian readers read this as Job acknowledging that speaking to God this way puts his life at risk.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the exact sense of the idiom is debated, but the general meaning is risk to life. Job knows that approaching God in protest is dangerous.

verses.text: Behold, he will kill me. I have no hope. Nevertheless, I will maintain my ways before him.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, he will kill me. I have no hope." Arminian readers note that the WEB reads the line as despair, yet Job adds, "Nevertheless, I will maintain my ways before him." He holds to integrity even without hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that other English translations render this verse as hope in God, and the line is read in more than one way. On either reading, Job keeps addressing God rather than turning away from him.

verses.text: This also will be my salvation, that a godless man will not come before him.
verses.arminianNotes: "This also will be my salvation, that a godless man will not come before him." Arminian readers see Job's confidence that his very willingness to face God shows he is not godless.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Job's reasoning: a hypocrite would not dare approach God. His desire to stand before God is itself evidence of sincerity, which the LORD later confirms.
